sections.title: Introduction and Testing Period
sections.content: RFC 255 reports on ARPANET host status from October 12 to October 22, 1971. The text notes that Monday, October 11 was Columbus Day and was not included. During these two weeks, the general status of hosts remained as it had been in the previous report, with no significant changes in server availability or host functionality.
sections.eli5: A report for the middle of October showed that computers stayed in the same state as before—the working ones kept working, and the broken ones stayed broken.

sections.title: Daily Test Results
sections.content: The report includes two tables of daily test results spanning October 12-22. Tests continued at random times during East Coast business hours using the same status codes: O for open, D for dead, T for timeout, H for half-open, and R for refused. Some sites marked times when they were not available for testing. UCLA's IBM-360/91 continued to offer only Remote Job Service, not a full Telnet server.
sections.eli5: The tables showed which computers answered on each day, using the same codes as the previous reports.

sections.title: Host Accessibility Patterns
sections.content: UCLA's SIGMA-7 and IBM-360/91, and UCSB's IBM-360/75 remained consistently accessible throughout the period. SRI's NIC PDP-10 was mostly open. Several hosts remained permanently dead or unreachable, including SRI's AI PDP-10 and SDC's IBM-360. Others showed variable behavior: MIT Multics ranged from open to dead to refused; Harvard PDP-10 was mostly dead; Lincoln IBM-360 was mostly half-open; and Utah and Stanford PDP-10s were frequently dead or timed out.
sections.eli5: The report showed which computers were reliable (UCLA and UCSB), which ones occasionally worked (MIT and Harvard), and which ones were consistently broken (Stanford and Utah).

references.text: Wentheimer, E., "Network host status", RFC 252, October 1971.
